sections.title: Image of God

questions.prompt: What does it mean for humans to bear God’s image?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human beings are appointed to represent God and exercise care over creation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human nature reflects divine attributes through capacities such as reason and moral agency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human beings are made for communion with God and one another.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The image is understood most fully through Christ, in whose likeness humanity is renewed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Has the fall changed whether a human being bears God’s image?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: The image remains, although how people reflect God is damaged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The image remains in one sense, while a likeness or original righteousness was lost and must be restored.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The image in the fullest sense is a calling realized only in union with Christ.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: If a person loses the capacity to reason or communicate, what happens to their standing as God’s image-bearer?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their standing is undiminished because the image belongs to human beings as such.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their standing is undiminished because it rests on God’s call and relation to them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both accounts fit my understanding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I understand “image” as a vocation or activity and would ground their undiminished dignity in another way.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

introduction: Capacity, relationship, and vocation offer different answers to what makes a human being an image-bearer.
editorialNotes: Separate the meaning of the image from whether a person can lose it. A person’s ability to exercise a capacity does not measure human worth.

furtherStudy.text: Baptist Faith and Message, article III, on humanity, the image of God, and dignity.

sections.title: Body and soul

questions.prompt: What kind of unity is a human being?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: An embodied person with an immaterial soul that can subsist apart from the body.

choices.label: B
choices.text: One living unity of matter and soul, with the soul as the form or life principle of the body.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A wholly physical person whom God can raise to life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A unity of body, soul, and spirit, with soul and spirit genuinely distinct.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scripture uses several terms for the whole person without settling a theory of composition.

choices.label: F
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: How does each person come to have an immaterial soul or spirit?
questions.displayNote: ↳ After ANT-04, if A or B or D is selected.

choices.label: A
choices.text: God directly creates each person’s soul.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human parents transmit the whole human nature, including its immaterial aspect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The person’s immaterial life emerges in the coming-to-be of the whole human being.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I affirm an immaterial aspect but have no settled view of its origin.

questions.prompt: Must a resurrected body have material continuity with the body that died?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. God raises and transforms that very body, however profoundly it changes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No. God can give the same person a newly constituted body without material continuity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: I affirm the resurrection of the same person but leave the question of material continuity open.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I understand resurrection chiefly as continued or renewed spiritual life.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: Do not derive a view of the intermediate state from a theory of human composition. ESCH treats the state of the dead separately.

furtherStudy.text: Compendium of the Catechism, questions 69–72, on body, soul, and the human person.

sections.title: Human freedom and the will

questions.prompt: For a choice to be free, must the person have been able to choose otherwise under exactly the same circumstances?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. A genuine alternative must have been possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No. Acting willingly for one’s own reasons can be free even if the choice was certain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Freedom requires that I be the source of my action, whether or not an alternative was possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I doubt one account of freedom fits every kind of choice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Suppose a person acts willingly from a character shaped by influences they never chose. What bears on their responsibility?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether the action expresses the person’s own intentions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the person could recognize and respond to moral reasons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether a different action was genuinely within reach.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether the person had meaningful agency in forming the habit or character involved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether coercion, compulsion, or diminished understanding impaired agency.

choices.label: F
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Can the redeemed be fully free in the life to come if they can no longer choose evil?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Freedom reaches its fullness when the will loves the good without division.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, if their fidelity remains freely theirs even though their falling away is certain never to occur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No. Meaningful freedom would still include a real ability to turn from the good.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I would leave the exact capacities of the resurrected will open.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: These questions concern agency in general. HAM and SOT separately ask what grace enables.

sections.title: Origin and nature of humanity

questions.prompt: What relationship do you see between God’s creation of human beings and biological ancestry?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: God created the first humans by a distinct act without biological descent from earlier life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: God brought human beings into existence through biological ancestry shared with other living things.

choices.label: C
choices.text: God used some continuity with earlier life alongside a special bodily creation of one or more first humans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I affirm God as creator while leaving the biological history open.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: How do you understand Adam in relation to the rest of humanity?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical individual from whom all humans are biologically descended.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical individual who represents humanity, whether or not all humans descend biologically from him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A figure representing humanity whose theological role does not require a historical individual.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I affirm the narrative’s teaching without deciding the historical question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: What would Adam’s historical existence establish about the earliest human population?
questions.displayNote: ↳ After ANT-10, if A or B is selected.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adam and Eve were the sole biological ancestors at the beginning of humanity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They could have lived within a larger population while becoming ancestors or representatives of others.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theological representation and population size are separate questions. I take no position on the latter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: Ask about divine creation, biological ancestry, and Adam’s representative role separately.

furtherStudy.text: BioLogos, “Were Adam and Eve Historical Figures?” Several models are distinguished within evolutionary creation.

sections.title: Human sexuality and marriage

questions.prompt: What significance does the creation of humans as male and female have for marriage?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sexual difference belongs to what constitutes a marriage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sexual difference is part of the creation account but is not necessary for every marriage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: I regard marriage principally as a social covenant and do not derive its definition from this passage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: What place does an unmarried life have in the human calling?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marriage and singleness can each be a complete vocation of Christian service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consecrated celibacy has a particular spiritual excellence alongside the goodness of marriage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marriage is the ordinary vocation. Lifelong singleness has a distinct calling only in particular circumstances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I do not think a person needs to identify a special vocation to live faithfully unmarried.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Does the creation of man and woman by itself establish an enduring order of authority in marriage?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Creation grounds an asymmetry of responsibility or headship as well as equal dignity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No. It grounds shared vocation and mutual partnership without establishing a standing hierarchy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: I would consider creation together with later biblical teaching before inferring any authority structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: Reserve specific judgments about conduct, divorce, and civil policy for Christian Ethics.

Enter at any dimension. In guided mode, begin with its opening question, continue through the main questions in the order shown, and insert a follow-up only when its stated answer matches. After the branch, resume with the next main question. A skipped answer or uncertainty opens no conditional branch unless specified.

Choose the closest single answer unless multiple selections are invited. On multiple-response questions, an uncertainty or “none” choice stands alone. Treat unresolved tensions as invitations to clarify.

vocabulary.definition: The study of human nature, vocation, freedom, and destiny in relation to God.
The special likeness or representative calling that Scripture ascribes to human beings in relation to God.
The view that a human being includes a physical body and an immaterial soul that can be distinguished from it.
A view of free choice that requires the choice to be undetermined by prior conditions, often understood as genuine ability to do otherwise.
The view that meaningful human freedom can coexist with determinism, such as when someone acts from their own reasons or desires.
